![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14227047/assets/720713e7e1dbfbc9ce3ebb486e8744327c633745d00df7dc862d794eefe57bbc.png)

What is the least distance between the curve $y=\sqrt{x}$ and the point $(4,0)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(4,0)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-0)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{x}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+(\sqrt{x})^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+16+x \\  & ={x}^{2}-7x+16.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-7 & =0 \\ 2x & =7 \\ x & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=\frac{7}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{7}{2}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(\frac{7}{2})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(\frac{7}{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-7(\frac{7}{2})+16} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{15}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the $y$-coordinate of the point on the curve $y={x}^{2}-2x$ that is closest to the point $(1,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(1,4)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-4)^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+{y}^{2}-8y+16 \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}-8y+17\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y={x}^{2}-2x.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(y) & =y+{y}^{2}-8y+17 \\  & ={y}^{2}-7y+17.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(y)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(y)=2y-7 & =0 \\ 2y & =7 \\ y & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(y)=2>0.$ Therefore, $y=\frac{7}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

So, the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) is minimized when $y=\frac{7}{2}.$

Find the least distance $d$ between the curve $y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}+1$ and the point $(2,1).$ Do not round the answer.

$d=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,1)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
S=(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}+1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}+1-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1})^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{x}^{2}+1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+{x}^{2}+1 \\  & =2{x}^{2}-4x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=4x-4 & =0 \\ 4x & =4 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=4>0,$ so $x=1$ gives a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=1$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(1)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(1)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(1)^{2}-4(1)+5} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,2)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{|x-1|}+2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{(\sqrt{|x-1|}+2-2)}^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+|x-1|.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\ge 1,$ we have $|x-1|=x-1,$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+x-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+x-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-3x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-3 & =0 \\ 2x & =3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S\,(\frac{3}{2})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S\,(\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-3(\frac{3}{2})+3} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}-\frac{9}{2}+3} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
